title: why bow three times?
hook: palms together, forehead to the floor, three times: who the bows are for, and why the incense
carry: bow to what wakes you up

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma, intention and what it grows. Today, a question a lot of people have at the altar: what am I doing when I bow?

Shoes off at the door. Palms together. Then down: knees, hands, forehead to the floor. Up. Again. And a third time. If you grew up going to temple, your body may know this before your mind ever asked why. Seen from outside, in a film or a yoga studio, it can look like worshiping a statue. It isn't quite that. The clue is the number three.
screen: `PALMS TOGETHER. FOREHEAD DOWN.` → `ONCE, TWICE, THREE TIMES.` → `WHY THREE?`

segments.voice: Each bow has a name, and together Buddhists call them the three jewels. The first is the Buddha: not a god, but a person who woke up. Many teachers say the bow is to that possibility of waking up, in anyone. The second is the Dharma, Dhamma in Pali: the teaching, and the way things actually are. The third is the Sangha: the community that practices it, monks and nuns, and in many places everyone walking the path together. Before chanting, many Buddhists say they go for refuge to these three, in Pali: Buddham saranam gacchami, I go to the Buddha for refuge, and so on for the other two. So the statue is a reminder, a bit like a photo of someone you love. And the incense? At a Buddhist altar it's offered as respect, not as something a god needs. One old verse says the scent of flowers only travels with the wind, but the goodness of a person travels even against it.
screen: `THE BUDDHA — ONE WHO WOKE UP` · `THE DHARMA — THE TEACHING` · `THE SANGHA — THE COMMUNITY` · `INCENSE — RESPECT, NOT FOOD FOR A GOD` · then, large: `THREE BOWS, THREE JEWELS.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Bring your palms together at your chest, if you like. Breathe in. As you breathe out, tip your head forward, just slightly: a small bow to whatever in you is trying to wake up.
The three jewels. The Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha: the one who woke up, the teaching, and the people who walk it. Second word.
Your line: bow to what wakes you up. Three bows, and none of them is to a statue. Day two, done.

howItsDone: At a temple or home shrine, many Buddhists bow three times, palms together, often touching knees, hands and forehead to the floor, to the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha; many light incense and recite the three refuges, Buddham saranam gacchami, before chanting.

story.title: the monk who bowed to everyone
story.text: A monk makes a whole town furious with one strange habit. He bows to everyone he meets, monks, nuns, strangers in the street, and tells each one: I would never look down on you, because you will become a buddha. People curse him. Some throw sticks and stones. He runs a little way off, turns around, and bows again from a safer distance. The story says he kept it up his whole life, and that he was the Buddha himself, in an earlier life.
story.source: the bodhisattva Never Disparaging, Lotus Sutra, chapter 20

notes: New lesson, written 2026-10-06 for the rebuilt week one (audience research: bowing and incense are things both audiences have done or seen without an explanation).

Bowing three times to the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha is widespread (Theravada, Chinese, Vietnamese, Korean and other temples) but not universal in form; the full bow is described generally ('knees, hands, forehead'). Confirm with Keepers from several communities.

'Many teachers say the bow is to that possibility of waking up, in anyone' leans toward a Mahayana/Zen framing; Theravada teachers often describe it as honoring the Buddha's qualities. Both are hedged as 'many teachers'. Confirm it's fair to both.

Incense: at Chinese and Vietnamese family altars incense is also offered to ancestors and local deities (a mix of Buddhist, Taoist and folk practice). The script limits its claim to 'at a Buddhist altar'. Confirm the wording.
Dhammapada 54 paraphrased ('the scent of flowers does not go against the wind… the fragrance of the good goes against the wind'); the voice does not name the text. Confirm.
Story: Never Disparaging (Sadaparibhuta), Lotus Sutra chapter 20 (Kumarajiva numbering); the Buddha identifies him as himself in a former life. Confirm the telling.
Pali refuge formula quoted from the original Pali (Khuddakapatha 1). The Dharma/Dhamma spelling: Dharma in the voice, with Dhamma given once; day 17 now matches.
